title: five-commands-the-map-cannot-render
author: CC
owner: CC builds it; each named charter's own owner gates its charter, and cairnmap owns the completeness rule being satisfied
intention: Five executables in bin/cmd — groundloop, mailcheck, operator, review, ruled — are commands no charter names, so the map cannot render them and the derivation gate reds. Each is named by the top-level `invoke` of the charter of the component its dispatcher actually execs, and /ruled is installed so the gate's sixth red clears too. No new charter is written: a thin dispatcher is not a component.
why: cairn/tools/cairnmap/cairnmap.py:336-351 walks bin/cmd and asks of each executable whether some charter's `invoke` names `cairn <name>`. The unnamed ones red with 'an undocumented command is impossible, by design' — the rule is that a command a reader cannot be briefed on does not exist for that reader, which is Law 5 at the command surface. Today five of 25 commands fail it, and the failure is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: skills/intent/proofs/test_intent_skill.py carries a tooth (test_the_skill_class_derivation_gate_is_green) that reads the whole gate, so /intent's own proof has been standing at 8/9 for as long as these five have been unnamed. A skill whose proof cannot go green is a skill whose seal is a hypothesis.
how: Five one-field edits and one symlink; nothing new is created. (1) cairn/devices/cairn/machines/ground_loop/intention+why.json — its `invoke` describes constructing GroundLoopDevice and names no command; append the operator face, `cairn groundloop status|start|stop|restart`, which bin/cmd/groundloop passes through verbatim to cairn.devices.cairn.machines.ground_loop.cli. (2) cairn/devices/cc/intention+why.json — carries NO `invoke` key at all; add one naming `cairn mailcheck`, because every byte that command reads is ~/.cairn/devices/cc/0/mail/, cc's own instance-space, and cc is therefore its owner even though the code sits in bin/cmd. (3) cairn/tools/operator_inbox/intention+why.json — `invoke` is the bare string 'cairn operator_inbox'; extend it to name `cairn operator` as well, the alias the whole corpus actually calls. (4) cairn/machines/skill_block/intention+why.json — its `invoke` already names `cairn skilldial`; add `cairn review` beside it, with its two forms (bare lists artifacts awaiting review; `cairn review <id> "words"` marks one reviewed). (5) skills/ruled/intention+why.json — `invoke` is '/ruled [<id>]', the slash face only; add the CLI face `cairn ruled [<id>]`, which execs skills.ruled.door. (6) Install /ruled: `ln -s ~/dev/src/cairn/skills/ruled ~/.claude/skills/ruled` — a symlink, matching all 14 standing entries; a copy would drift silently. (7) Poke cairn/tools/intentions_model_compiler/recompile_gate.sh once, after the charter edits, before the crossing.
falsifier: DONE when (1) `./bin/cairn cairnmap --gate` exits 0 with zero findings across all seven checks; (2) each of the five commands is named by the top-level `invoke` of the charter of the component its dispatcher execs, and each such invoke carries the command's REAL usage — a checkable shape within 80 characters of the named command: a `<placeholder>`, a `sub|command` alternation, or the explicit words "no arguments" — so the gate's mention-check cannot be satisfied by a bare word. (REFINED DURING THE BUILD, 2026-09-11, and named here because the cast bar was unsatisfiable: the clause first read "at minimum one subcommand or argument the dispatcher actually accepts", and `bin/cmd/mailcheck` accepts NONE — it is a self-contained reader that takes no arguments. A bar no honest charter for mailcheck could clear would have forced either a false invoke or an exemption; the third shape admits the true answer instead, and still refuses a bare word.); (3) `python3 skills/intent/proofs/test_intent_skill.py` prints 13/13 teeth green (9 standing teeth plus the four this ticket declares), which requires /ruled installed as well as named; and (4) no new intention+why.json exists anywhere under bin/cmd/. WRONG INTENT if five charters appear under bin/cmd/ — a thin dispatcher is not a component, five new charters inflate the census by five with nothing behind them, and the design of `cairn groundloop` would then live somewhere other than where a mind stands to be briefed on the ground loop (Law 5). WRONG INTENT if /ruled is installed by copying rather than symlinking.

traces_to: Law 5 (intent, state and proofs share an address, and the address carries what a mind needs NOW — a command whose design is written nowhere near it cannot brief the mind standing there, which is what 'an undocumented command is impossible, by design' means); Law 8 (nothing enters proven-space without a proof a hollow build could not pass — /intent's proof has stood at 8/9, so its green was never fully earned); Law 9 (red is the default and these five have been red since they were written); Law 1 (a reader re-deriving what `cairn review` does by reading the dispatcher is re-deriving a settled answer).
known_hole_inherited_knowingly: THE COMMAND LANE WALKS ONE WAY, and this ticket does not turn it around. It asks whether each executable in bin/cmd is named by some charter; it never asks whether each command a charter NAMES still exists. So a charter naming a command nobody can run is invisible. n=1 and it is inside this ticket's own scope: cairn/tools/operator_inbox's charter has named `cairn operator_inbox` while every caller in the corpus says `cairn operator`, and nothing ever reported it. The inverse check is NOT built here because extracting `cairn <word>` from prose invoke strings false-positives on bin's own literal `cairn <name> <args...>`, and a check that manufactures reds is worse than the gap. Recorded for a later cast.

decisions.text: (landed) cairn/devices/cairn/machines/ground_loop/intention+why.json top-level 'invoke' (a single string) ENDS with the sentence: CLI: `cairn groundloop status|start|stop|restart` (bin/cmd/groundloop, a dispatcher into `python3 -m cairn.devices.cairn.machines.ground_loop.cli`) — followed by one clause per subcommand. The alternation status|start|stop|restart is the 'real usage' shape clause (2) demands. No other key was added. THE PER-SUBCOMMAND CLAUSES, VERBATIM: The per-subcommand clauses are these exact words, one string, following the dispatcher line: — `status` reads the liveness record and prints LIVE|DEAD with its age, `start` launches the resident beat (and refuses with exit 3 if one is already resident, which is why it is safe to type twice), `stop` sends the SIGTERM the resident exits cleanly on, `restart` is the two in order. The command is the ONLY face an operator needs; the Python face above is for proofs and for a device wiring its own shim. (This is the landed text at cairn/devices/cairn/machines/ground_loop/intention+why.json, commit 8d8bbe62; nothing further follows it.) PRESERVE THE PRIOR PYTHON FACE DESCRIPTION AND APPEND THE CLI SECTION — nothing before 'CLI:' was changed. THE COMPLETE INVOKE STRING AS LANDED (commit 8d8bbe62; Python face first, then the CLI section; the string ends where this quotation ends): Construct: `gl = GroundLoopDevice()` (anonymous, no device space — what proofs build) or `GroundLoopDevice(liveness_home=liveness.instance_home())` (the resident singleton — every beat touches its record). A device subscribes its shim: `gl.subscribe(shim)` (idempotent by device_id; only a shim — device_id + on_pulse — may subscribe). Beat: `gl.beat(now, context)` pulses every subscribed shim once and returns a legible beat-record. `now` is passed explicitly, so the pulse is provable without a clock. Run resident: `python3 -m cairn.devices.cairn.machines.ground_loop` (the thin wall-clock backing, ruled 1s cadence, SIGTERM-clean; SELF-GUARDING — a second launch refuses with exit 3, naming what the record said, so spawning it is always safe). Ask liveness: `liveness.read_liveness(now)` → {verdict LIVE|DEAD, record, age_s}. Prove: `python3 cairn/devices/cairn/machines/ground_loop/proofs/test_ground_loop.py` (exit 0 = green). CLI: `cairn groundloop status|start|stop|restart` (bin/cmd/groundloop, a dispatcher into `python3 -m cairn.devices.cairn.machines.ground_loop.cli`) — `status` reads the liveness record and prints LIVE|DEAD with its age, `start` launches the resident beat (and refuses with exit 3 if one is already resident, which is why it is safe to type twice), `stop` sends the SIGTERM the resident exits cleanly on, `restart` is the two in order. The command is the ONLY face an operator needs; the Python face above is for proofs and for a device wiring its own shim.

def test_clause_1_the_command_lane_carries_no_reds():
    """Falsifier clause (1), read against THIS tree rather than against the host.

    `cairnmap.inspect(repo=REPO)` runs the same predicate the CLI gate runs — for each
    executable in bin/cmd, a `\bcairn <name>\b` search across every charter'd unit's
    invoke — but over the repo this file is standing in. That is what lets the tooth run
    inside `cairn test --hollow`'s worktree, where the CLI reads a repo that isn't there.

    Only the command lane is read. The commons-reading lanes beside it legitimately red
    in a worktree (commons_root() is name-based too), and collapsing 'this lane is
    clean' into 'the gate is green' would make the tooth unreadable exactly where it is
    needed most (Law 7 — a diagnostic surface may not collapse an error).
    """
    from cairn.tools.cairnmap import cairnmap
    entry = [e for e in cairnmap.inspect(repo=REPO)
             if e["identity"] == "every_command_is_named_by_a_charter"]
    assert len(entry) == 1, f"the command lane did not run at all: {entry}"
    reds = entry[0]["values"]["reds"]
    assert reds == [], "commands no charter's invoke names:\n  " + "\n  ".join(reds)
    # NON-VACUITY, and it is the whole reason this tooth can be trusted inside a
    # worktree. A lane that found no commands reds nothing and looks identical to a lane
    # that found twenty-five and owned them all. The CLI's worktree run failed exactly
    # this way: 0 charters, command lane 'pass'.
    expected = entry[0]["expected"]
    assert len(expected) >= 20, (
        f"the lane walked {len(expected)} command(s) — it found no corpus, so its green "
        f"says nothing: {expected}")
    assert set(COMMAND_OWNERS) <= set(expected), (
        f"the six this ticket is about are not among the commands walked: {expected}")


def test_clause_2_the_five_are_named_with_real_usage():
    """Falsifier clause (2): named by the RIGHT charter, and with usage a bare word
    cannot fake.

    Clause (1) only asks whether SOME charter mentions the command — a charter anywhere
    in the corpus could claim `cairn review` and the lane would go green. This tooth
    pins the mention to the charter of the component the dispatcher execs, and to that
    charter's OWN top-level invoke rather than a facility block, so 'owned' means the
    thing a reader would go and read.
    """
    for name, rel in sorted(COMMAND_OWNERS.items()):
        invoke = _invoke_of(rel)
        assert invoke, f"{rel} carries no top-level `invoke` at all, so it names nothing"
        hits = [m for m in re.finditer(rf"\bcairn {re.escape(name)}\b", invoke)]
        assert hits, (
            f"`cairn {name}` is not named by its own component's invoke ({rel}) — the "
            f"lane may still be green off some other charter, which is the substitution "
            f"this clause exists to catch")
        # At least ONE mention must carry usage in its window. `cairn review` appears
        # twice in skill_block's invoke — the bare listing form and the marking form —
        # and only the second carries an argument; either satisfying is correct.
        assert any(_USAGE_SHAPE.search(invoke[m.end():m.end() + _USAGE_WINDOW])
                   for m in hits), (
            f"`cairn {name}` is named in {rel} with no real usage within "
            f"{_USAGE_WINDOW} chars — no <placeholder>, no sub|command alternation, and "
            f"no explicit 'no arguments'. A bare mention satisfies the gate's lane and "
            f"tells a reader nothing, which is the measured state of `cairn "
            f"operator_inbox` before this ticket.")


def test_clause_3_ruled_is_installed_as_a_symlink_and_names_its_cli_face():
    """Falsifier clause (3)'s two halves, and the WRONG INTENT clause that rides it.

    The gate's sixth red is not a command-lane red at all — /ruled carries a charter and
    has no entry in ~/.claude/skills — but the host-wide tooth below reads the WHOLE
    gate, so it cannot go green until this clears. A COPY would clear the gate and fork
    the source; the ticket names that as WRONG INTENT, and all 14 pre-existing entries
    are symlinks, so the install pattern is not in question.

    The install half is host state and survives a repo reversion by construction; the
    charter half does not, which is what gives this tooth something to say about the
    build.
    """
    from cairn.tools.cairnmap import cairnmap
    installed = cairnmap.installed_skills()
    assert "ruled" in installed, (
        f"/ruled is chartered and not installed — the derivation gate's sixth finding. "
        f"Installed: {sorted(installed)}")
    link = Path.home() / ".claude" / "skills" / "ruled"
    assert link.is_symlink(), (
        f"{link} exists but is not a symlink — a copied skill forks its own source, and "
        f"every one of the other {len(installed) - 1} entries is a link")
    target = installed["ruled"]
    assert target is not None and (target / "SKILL.md").is_file(), (
        f"the /ruled link resolves to {target}, which carries no SKILL.md")
    # The repo half: the charter must record the CLI face beside the slash face. Both
    # are real — bin/cmd/ruled execs skills.ruled.door directly — and a charter naming
    # only one of a component's two faces is a charter a reader cannot run from.
    invoke = _invoke_of(COMMAND_OWNERS["ruled"])
    assert "/ruled" in invoke and re.search(r"\bcairn ruled\b", invoke), (
        f"the /ruled charter records only one of its two faces: {invoke!r}")


def test_clause_4_no_charter_was_minted_under_bin_cmd():
    """The ticket's WRONG INTENT clause, head on: five charters appearing under bin/cmd
    would clear the gate by manufacturing five components that are not components.

    A dispatcher is a two-line exec into a component that already has a charter; giving
    it one of its own would make the complexity axis say there are five more things in
    the system than there are. This tooth contributes no reversion signal (nothing this
    build writes can make it red) and is declared anyway, because the clause is a bound
    on the SHAPE of the fix and an unwatched bound is the one a later hand crosses.
    """
    minted = sorted(str(p.relative_to(REPO)) for p in (REPO / "bin" / "cmd").rglob("intention+why.json"))
    assert minted == [], f"charters minted under bin/cmd: {minted}"
